Joint, Decoupled, or Agent: When Each Multimodal Alignment Paradigm Wins

Yi Fang1   Gaurav Srivastava1   Sirui Ding2   Xuan Wang1 1Department of Computer Science Virginia Tech Blacksburg, VA, USA {yif,gks,xuanw}@vt.edu    2Department of Biomedical Data Science Stanford University Stanford, CA, USA srding@stanford.edu ††thanks: Corresponding author: xuanw@vt.edu.
Abstract

Jointly pretrained multimodal encoders are a common way to combine modalities, while alternatives integrate their information during downstream training or inference. When does each approach win? We compare three paradigms, instantiated with public checkpoints, across 16 paired datasets in five domains and multiple training-label budgets. Joint trains a fusion head on frozen, jointly pretrained encoders. Decoupled trains a fusion head on frozen, independently pretrained encoders. Agent gives a frozen LLM task instructions, labelled examples, available sample text, and supervised unimodal readouts. No paradigm dominates the complete 144144 dataset–budget combinations: Decoupled wins 5454, Joint 4444, and Agent 4646 by mean utility. ScienceQA, MELD, and MetMeme shift from Agent to fusion as supervision increases. Between the fusion paradigms, Joint leads on four of five QA datasets across all evaluated budgets, while higher unimodal 55-NN accuracy is associated with a relative shift toward Decoupled across eight classification datasets (Spearman ρ=−0.67\rho=-0.67). We test whether representation and task diagnostics predict these preferences on held-out datasets before fitting their candidate systems. A two-step cascade combines these diagnostics with task and budget metadata to select Agent or fusion, then Joint or Decoupled. Under leave-one-group-out evaluation, it selects the winner in 71.4%71.4\% of cells versus 54.2%54.2\% for metadata-only routing, with mean relative regret 0.0280.028 versus 0.0570.057. Using geometry, supervised representation diagnostics, and text–label matching together yields higher accuracy and lower regret than using any one of these sources with metadata. These results connect paradigm preferences to supervision budget, task format, and unimodal 55-NN accuracy. Target-task diagnostics thus support selecting among the three paradigms before candidate fitting.

1 Introduction

Multimodal systems are increasingly assembled from pretrained components. Vision–language, audio–language, biomedical, molecular, and protein–ligand settings all expose encoders or paired representation models that can be reused for downstream tasks (Radford et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2023b; Gorantla et al., 2025). A central design choice is when and how to integrate the modalities. Given paired inputs and a downstream label, cross-modal information can enter through jointly pretrained representations (Joint), supervised fusion of independently pretrained encoders (Decoupled), or inference-time composition by an LLM reading unimodal outputs and available text (Agent). We call Joint and Decoupled the fusion paradigms. Decoupled only learns task-specific fusion on independently pretrained encoders; Joint initializes its frozen encoders from paired pretraining and then learns task-specific fusion. Agent adds LLM inference to supervised readouts.

Choosing among these paradigms requires relating the target task to the available representations and supervision. We study when their preferences change and whether target-task diagnostics can predict those preferences before fitting the candidate systems.

We benchmark the three paradigms on 1616 paired datasets in five domains, varying each dataset’s training-label budget. Each domain has a default encoder pair per fusion paradigm. Agent uses the same unimodal encoders as Decoupled. We match encoder architecture and scale where available, retaining the pretrained representations.

Three patterns connect paradigm preference to supervision budget, task format, and unimodal 55-NN accuracy. ScienceQA, MELD, and MetMeme shift from Agent to fusion as supervision increases. AI2D and CUB retain their preferred paradigms across the evaluated budgets. Among fusion systems, candidate-matching QA usually favors jointly pretrained encoders. In classification, higher unimodal 55-NN accuracy is associated with a relative preference for independently pretrained encoders, suggesting that task-relevant information already present in each modality can support effective downstream fusion (Section 3.3).

Component comparisons show that a paradigm win can coexist with little benefit from integration. On AI2D, LLM-only exceeds the full Agent; on CUB, the visual probe nearly matches Decoupled. Readouts improve Agent accuracy on ScienceQA and VQA-RAD (Section 3.2).

We predict preferences among the three alignment paradigms from representation geometry, supervised representation diagnostics, text–label matching, and task and budget metadata. A two-step cascade first selects Agent versus fusion, then Joint versus Decoupled. On held-out datasets, the cascade improves selection accuracy and reduces relative regret over metadata-only routing and a task-and-budget lookup. Feature ablations assess their contributions (Section 3.3).

Our contributions are (1) a comparison of three multimodal alignment paradigms under common target-task and budget protocols, identifying preferences associated with supervision budget, task format, and unimodal 55-NN accuracy, (2) component controls and implementation variants that assess the gains from integration and the stability of paradigm preferences, and (3) held-out-dataset evidence that representation and task diagnostics improve paradigm selection before candidate adaptation, supported by metadata baselines and diagnostic-group ablations.

2 Method

We compare three pretrained alignment paradigms on paired target observations, define their utility and selection protocol, and predict the preferred paradigm with a two-step cascade.

2.1 Three Alignment Paradigms

Let 𝒟d={(xi(a),xi(b),yi)}i=1nd\mathcal{D}_{d}=\{(x_{i}^{(a)},x_{i}^{(b)},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{d}} be a paired dataset. At budget KK, seed s∈{0,…,4}s\in\{0,\ldots,4\} determines the labelled training set 𝒮d,K(s)\mathcal{S}_{d,K}^{(s)} and head initialization. All paradigms share the full test split 𝒬d\mathcal{Q}_{d} and a disjoint development split 𝒱d\mathcal{V}_{d}, fixed across budgets, heads, and seeds. Budget KK excludes development labels: fitting and selection use |𝒮d,K(s)|+|𝒱d||\mathcal{S}_{d,K}^{(s)}|+|\mathcal{V}_{d}| labels. For metric mdm_{d} with direction sd∈{+1,−1}s_{d}\in\{+1,-1\}, define

Uℛ​(f)=sd​md​((f⁡(x),y)(x,y)∈ℛ),U⁡(p,d,K)=15​∑s=04U𝒬d​(fp,d,K(s)),U_{\mathcal{R}}(f)=s_{d}\,m_{d}\!\left((f(x),y)_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{R}}\right),\qquad U(p;d,K)=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{s=0}^{4}U_{\mathcal{Q}_{d}}\!\left(f_{p,d,K}^{(s)}\right), (1)

where mdm_{d} is accuracy or MAE. Utilities are comparable only within a cell and exclude deployment cost. For the candidate set 𝒫={Joint,Decoupled,Agent}\mathcal{P}=\{\textsc{Joint},\textsc{Decoupled},\textsc{Agent}\}, let U⋆​(d,K)=maxp∈𝒫⁡U⁡(p,d,K)U^{\star}(d,K)=\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}U(p;d,K). Routing accuracy and regret use this candidate set. LLM-only and unimodal probes assess component value (Section 3.2).

Fusion Heads

Joint and Decoupled both train a fusion head on a frozen encoder pair (Ga,Gb)(G_{a},G_{b}). The head consists of a fusion operator ψω\psi_{\omega}, drawn from a search space Ψ\Psi of eight standard architectures (Appendix C.3), followed by a task head hθh_{\theta}. For each ψ∈Ψ\psi\in\Psi, parameters are fit on the labelled set (suppressing seed indices here),

(ωψ⋆,θψ⋆)=arg​minω,θ∑(x,y)∈𝒮d,Kℓd(hθ(ψω(Ga(x(a)),Gb(x(b)))),y).(\omega_{\psi}^{\star},\theta_{\psi}^{\star})\;=\;\argmin_{\omega,\theta}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{S}_{d,K}}\ell_{d}\!\bigl(h_{\theta}\!\bigl(\psi_{\omega}(G_{a}(x^{(a)}),G_{b}(x^{(b)}))\bigr),\,y\bigr). (2)

For classification and regression, select hyperparameters and checkpoints on 𝒱d\mathcal{V}_{d} within each head ψ\psi (Table 24). QA uses a fixed optimization configuration with development-based checkpoint selection (Appendix C.3). For each seed, then select the head:

ψ^p,d,K(s)=arg​maxψ∈Ψ⁡U𝒱d​(fp,ψ,d,K(s)),fp,d,K(s)=fp,ψ^p,d,K(s),d,K(s).\hat{\psi}_{p,d,K}^{(s)}=\argmax_{\psi\in\Psi}U_{\mathcal{V}_{d}}\!\left(f_{p,\psi,d,K}^{(s)}\right),\qquad f_{p,d,K}^{(s)}=f_{p,\hat{\psi}_{p,d,K}^{(s)},d,K}^{(s)}. (3)

The five selected models determine the mean utilities and routing targets. For QA, Eq. (2) uses a shared scalar scorer for each image–candidate or molecule–candidate pair, with cross-entropy over candidate scores. For image QA, each candidate text concatenates the question and answer.

Joint: Alignment at Pretraining

Joint sets (Ga,Gb)=(FJa,FJb)(G_{a},G_{b})=(F_{J}^{a},F_{J}^{b}) in Eq. (2), using towers jointly pretrained on paired multimodal data.

Decoupled: Supervised Fusion of Unaligned Encoders

Decoupled uses independently pretrained unimodal encoders Ea:𝒳a→ℝraE_{a}:\mathcal{X}_{a}\to\mathbb{R}^{r_{a}} and Eb:𝒳b→ℝrbE_{b}:\mathcal{X}_{b}\to\mathbb{R}^{r_{b}}, never aligned to each other, and sets (Ga,Gb)=(Ea,Eb)(G_{a},G_{b})=(E_{a},E_{b}) in Eq. (2). Matching controls architecture family and scale (Definition 1), not pretraining histories. Supervised fusion need not create a shared embedding space.

Agent: LLM-Based Inference-Time Composition

Agent combines a frozen instruction-tuned LLM with readouts ga,gbg_{a},g_{b} using the same frozen Ea,EbE_{a},E_{b} as Decoupled. Trainable readouts are fitted separately per seed on 𝒮d,K\mathcal{S}_{d,K} and selected on 𝒱d\mathcal{V}_{d}. For image MCQ, the image readout is a trained bilinear candidate scorer, while the text readout uses unscaled text–option cosine similarity without a fitted head (Appendix E.1). Outputs are per-candidate scores for classification/QA and scalar predictions for regression. The LLM receives task instruction ℐd\mathcal{I}_{d}, up to ten labelled in-context examples ℰd,K⊂𝒮d,K\mathcal{E}_{d,K}\subset\mathcal{S}_{d,K}, readout outputs oa,obo_{a},o_{b}, and raw sample text x(t)x^{(t)} when available. Non-text inputs reach it only through readouts. For KIBA and PDBbind, x(t)x^{(t)} contains ligand SMILES. The LLM returns a task answer, parsed into a class, candidate index, or regression value:

fAgent,d,K​(x)=parse⁡(πLLM​(ℐd,ℰd,K,x(t),oa,ob)).f_{\textsc{Agent},d,K}(x)=\mathrm{parse}\bigl(\pi_{\mathrm{LLM}}(\mathcal{I}_{d},\mathcal{E}_{d,K},x^{(t)},o_{a},o_{b})\bigr). (4)

Inline-1 supplies both readouts in one greedy-decoding turn. Utility averages the same five labelled-set seeds as Decoupled (Appendix E). Readouts and demonstrations depend on the labelled set, making Agent performance budget-dependent even with a frozen LLM.

Prerequisites and Tie Band

All paradigms use paired target inputs. Decoupled needs paired labels for fusion and Joint also needs a paired-pretrained checkpoint. Agent fits its trainable readouts separately on these paired target observations. Our tie convention Agent≺Decoupled≺Joint\textsc{Agent}\prec\textsc{Decoupled}\prec\textsc{Joint} prioritizes fewer cross-modal training requirements. For tolerance ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, let

𝒯ϵ​(d,K)={p:U⋆​(d,K)−U⁡(p,d,K)≤ϵd},ϵd=ϵ​|U⋆​(d,K)|,\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}(d,K)\;=\;\bigl\{\,p:U^{\star}(d,K)-U(p;d,K)\leq\epsilon_{d}\,\bigr\},\qquad\epsilon_{d}=\epsilon\,|U^{\star}(d,K)|, (5)

be the paradigms within tolerance. The earliest in the preference order is the target. ϵ=0\epsilon=0 selects a maximizer. The tolerance ϵ\epsilon specifies an application-defined utility margin. Main-table raw counts instead use maximum utility, assigning exact fusion ties to Decoupled.

2.2 Feature Extraction

The features combine representation geometry, supervised representation diagnostics (two ANOVA and three 55-NN features), a text diagnostic, and task and budget metadata (Table 28). Geometry describes the structure within each representation and the correspondence between modalities. ANOVA and 55-NN assess how target labels organize these representations and how well local neighbours recover them, providing task-specific evidence about the inputs available to supervised fusion.

These features use frozen Ea,EbE_{a},E_{b} embeddings and labels from 𝒮d,K\mathcal{S}_{d,K}, except mutual-kNN, which uses up to 8,0008{,}000 paired observations from the full training pool. Per-side geometry enters as minimum and maximum values. CKA, mutual-kNN, and concatenated kNN require paired observations. Feature definitions and inputs appear in Appendix D.1 and Table 29.

The composite text diagnostic combines label-name matching and supervised text-neighbour prediction. For classification with CC classes,

Δzs​(𝒮)=norm⁡(aTL)−norm⁡(akNNtext),norm⁡(a)=a−1/C1−1/C.\Delta_{\mathrm{zs}}(\mathcal{S})=\operatorname{norm}(a_{\mathrm{TL}})-\operatorname{norm}(a_{\mathrm{kNN}}^{\mathrm{text}}),\qquad\operatorname{norm}(a)=\frac{a-1/C}{1-1/C}. (6)

Here aTLa_{\mathrm{TL}} is cosine-nearest-class-name accuracy using a fixed BGE-M3 text probe. akNNtexta_{\mathrm{kNN}}^{\mathrm{text}} is leave-one-out 55-NN accuracy in the default Decoupled text embedding. The label-name term uses up to 2020 sampled examples from 𝒮d,K\mathcal{S}_{d,K}; the neighbour term uses the labelled set capped at 8,0008{,}000 rows, so the two accuracies can be evaluated on different subsets. Regression instead uses −r-r, the Pearson correlation of text-side 55-NN predictions. QA uses zero because options vary by question. This diagnostic receives no size residualization. For classification, its design asks whether label semantics support prediction beyond local text-neighbour evidence. This motivates its use in the Agent/Fusion decision, where the LLM interprets sample text and label names alongside readouts. Its predictive contribution is evaluated through the feature ablations. Appendix D.2 gives implementation details.

2.3 Two-Step Cascade

The hierarchy follows the paradigms' shared components: Joint and Decoupled use supervised fusion of frozen embeddings, while Agent adds LLM composition of text and readouts. It first separates these integration procedures, then distinguishes the fusion encoders' pretraining source. Step 1 asks whether Agent is competitive. Otherwise Step 2 chooses between Joint and Decoupled. Each step selects diagnostics and budget features alongside mandatory task indicators.

Step 1 learns Agent/Fusion labels on all cells under Eq. (5). Step 2 learns Joint/Decoupled labels on Fusion cells (Appendix C.8).

Feature Processing and Selection

Supervised representation diagnostics are residualized against log10⁡|𝒮d,K|\log_{10}|\mathcal{S}_{d,K}|, separately for regression and other tasks. Step 1 always includes regression and QA indicators; Step 2 always includes the QA indicator. The text diagnostic Δzs\Delta_{\mathrm{zs}} is mandatory in Step 1. Each step selects a budget block containing all descriptors, all except budget fraction, or none. The symbolic-sequence indicator is a ranked candidate in both steps.

Residualization and Laplacian ranking are fitted once per outer fold using diagnostics from all outer-training datasets, including inner-validation groups, without paradigm-winner labels. Inner selection of feature width and budget block uses these fixed transformations; imputation, missingness indicators, standardization, and classifiers are refitted within each training partition. The outer-held-out dataset enters only at prediction time. Appendix C.8 specifies the full procedure.

Classifier and Decision

Each step uses L2-regularized logistic regression (C=1C=1), with decision score st​(x)=wt⊤​ϕt​(x)+bts_{t}(x)=w_{t}^{\top}\phi_{t}(x)+b_{t}. Grouped cross-validation on the outer training set gives out-of-fold scores ot,io_{t,i}. For the step's training positive-label fraction πt\pi_{t}, the threshold is

τt=Q1−πt​({ot,i}),t∈{1,2}.\tau_{t}=Q_{1-\pi_{t}}\!\left(\{o_{t,i}\}\right),\qquad t\in\{1,2\}. (7)

Step 2 computes its prior and score quantile on Fusion-labelled cells. The quantile threshold approximately matches the positive rate on the pooled out-of-fold scores to the training prior, with deviations from finite samples and tied scores. The cascade predicts

p^​(d,K,ϵ)={Agent,s1≥τ1,Joint,s1<τ1​and​s2≥τ2,Decoupled,otherwise.\hat{p}(d,K;\epsilon)=\begin{cases}\textsc{Agent},&s_{1}\geq\tau_{1},\\ \textsc{Joint},&s_{1}<\tau_{1}\ \text{and}\ s_{2}\geq\tau_{2},\\ \textsc{Decoupled},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (8)

Final classifiers fit the outer training groups and use these independently determined thresholds.

Evaluation Methodology

We evaluate 144144 dataset–budget combinations from 1616 datasets in 1515 groups: DrugBank-Desc and DrugBank-Pharma are always held out together, in both outer evaluation and inner selection. Each held-out cell reads one labelled-set feature seed per run. Results average five runs, while training cells use five-seed feature means. Targets use the mean candidate utilities and are re-derived at each ϵ\epsilon. We report cell-weighted winner accuracy and relative regret (U⋆−U⁡(p^))/|U⋆|(U^{\star}-U(\hat{p}))/|U^{\star}|. The paired-bootstrap protocol uses 4,0004{,}000 bootstrap draws of the 1515 groups, keeping all budgets and seeds of a selected group together (Appendix C.7).

3 Experiments

We examine budget-dependent preferences, input contributions, and prediction of paradigm choice. Appendix A expands these analyses.

Experimental Setup

We evaluate 1616 paired datasets across five domains and three formats (classification, regression, QA). We vary training budget KK under the protocol in Section 2.1. Shots are per class or regression quantile bucket, so 2020-shot can exceed 10%10\% in label count (Table 27). A cell is one dataset–budget combination. Main tables report 4848 cells at three budgets per dataset. Routing uses 144144 dataset–budget combinations over the full grids. Encoder pairs are in Appendix B. The default Agent uses Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2025).

3.1 Paradigm Preferences Depend on Task and Supervision

Paradigm preferences can persist or reverse as supervision increases.

Tables 1 and 2 report accuracy and MAE for 4848 dataset–budget cells. Figure 1 summarizes wins over all 144144 cells in the full budget grids. Across full budget grids, AI2D favors Agent, CUB favors Decoupled, and DrugBank-Desc favors Joint. ScienceQA instead shifts from Agent to Joint, while CrisisMMD returns to Agent at full budget (Figure 2). MELD and MetMeme also move from Agent at 2020-shot to fusion with larger training sets. Budget effects can be non-monotonic.

Most paradigm preferences are consistent across seeds.

On the fixed test splits, the same paradigm wins strictly across all five training seeds in about 79%79\% of the main-table cells (Table 5).

Performance margins vary substantially relative to inference cost.

Estimated Agent inference FLOPs are approximately 360360–3,0003{,}000 times those of fusion. For classification and QA, its mean advantage over the better fusion system ranges from marginal to substantial. Appendix G reports the gain distribution, full-grid relative margins, and routing costs.

3.2 Input Interventions and Implementation Sensitivity

Matched controls and implementation variants test component value and preference stability.

3.2.1 Text and Readouts Have Task-Dependent Value

Readout information does not always improve QA accuracy.

Controls use the main-table full-budget samples and five-seed aggregation (Table 13). LLM-only exceeds all three paradigms only on AI2D (0.8300.830 versus 0.7780.778 for Agent). Readouts improve ScienceQA and VQA-RAD means by 1.41.4 and 7.57.5 points. Yet full Agent exceeds shuffled readouts by 11.811.8, 7.97.9, and 7.57.5 points on these three tasks (Figure 3). On AI2D, omitting readouts beats both informative and shuffled scores.

Food101 readout gains are 2.9/2.8/0.82.9/2.8/0.8 points at 2020-shot/10%10\%/100%100\%, over LLM-only’s 0.843/0.852/0.8980.843/0.852/0.898 (Table 14). Agent wins throughout, with diminishing readout gains.

Readouts remain useful even without informative label names.

CUB and OxfordPet retain 0.6000.600 and 0.6320.632 under anonymised labels, above LLM-only and shuffled controls.

Raw question and option text contribute to QA performance.

Deleting only the question body yields 0.602/0.545/0.2050.602/0.545/0.205 on AI2D/ScienceQA/VQA-RAD. Removing question and option contents lowers these to 0.325/0.372/0.1850.325/0.372/0.185.

Component controls show where integration adds value.

Score averaging without the LLM trails Agent by 9.69.6–24.924.9 points on the reported Agent-winning classification settings (Appendix A.8). CUB's visual probe nearly matches Decoupled at full budget (0.916/0.9170.916/0.917; Table 9).

3.2.2 Preferences Also Depend on the Candidate Implementations

Fusion-head choice strongly affects MCQ accuracy.

At full budget, the diagnostic best–worst head spread is 0.110.11–0.580.58 on MCQ versus 0.0060.006–0.130.13 on classification (Figure 7). Restricting Joint to concat reverses the PDBbind winner. These spreads show why head selection matters when comparing the fusion paradigms.

The value of domain specialization depends on the encoder configuration.

On Fracture, biomedical Joint checkpoints outperform general CLIP by up to 9.79.7 points, whereas neither Rad-DINO nor Phikon improves Decoupled over DINOv2 (Figure 10). These variants change architecture as well as pretraining (Appendix B.5).

Providing both readouts usually outperforms single-tool selection.

Across the seven classification datasets with both readouts available to the Multi-2 controller, at three budgets, supplying both readouts in one turn (Inline-1) usually beats requesting one in multiple turns (Multi-2). On CUB, Multi-2 selects the text readout on 79%79\% of examples, and mean accuracy across budgets falls from about 0.860.86 to 0.160.16 (Figure 13).

Paradigm preferences are largely stable across capable LLMs, but a tiny controller performs poorly.

Gemma-3-27B-it leads on CUB and OxfordPet across reported budgets, and Qwen3-32B on Food101. Across tasks and budgets evaluated with all four LLMs, the Agent–fusion preference usually remains unchanged (Figure 12). SmolLM2-135M never outperforms the better fusion system in its evaluated classification and QA settings and has a mean parse-failure rate near 90%90\%, indicating difficulty following the answer protocol (Appendix A.8).

In-context examples do not consistently improve performance.

In-context examples yield less than one accuracy point on average but help MetMeme by 9.99.9 points at 2020-shot and hurt OxfordPet by 5.75.7 points at 10%10\%. Across all eight classification datasets at three budgets, removing examples usually preserves the preferred paradigm, even when accuracy changes substantially (Figure 11).

3.3 Diagnostics of Paradigm Preference and Grouped Prediction

Task format and unimodal 55-NN accuracy relate to fusion preference.

Figure 4 connects two diagnostics to paradigm preference. Across all budgets, Joint exceeds Decoupled on four of five QA datasets, whose fusion heads perform candidate matching. VQA-RAD favors Decoupled or ties. Across eight classification datasets, higher unimodal 55-NN accuracy is associated with a smaller Joint-minus-Decoupled margin (Spearman ρ=−0.67\rho=-0.67). Each point represents one dataset, averaging over matched budget cells. The horizontal axis uses the stronger modality's five-seed mean 55-NN accuracy; the vertical axis averages the Joint–Decoupled utility difference normalized by the best of all three paradigms. The association remains negative under dataset deletion and chance normalization (Appendix A.13).

Table 3 evaluates prediction of the preferred member of {Joint,Decoupled,Agent}\{\textsc{Joint},\textsc{Decoupled},\textsc{Agent}\} on 144144 dataset–budget combinations in 1515 held-out groups. Metadata-only routing measures the added value of diagnostics; Direct and the other classifiers test alternative predictors.

Diagnostics add predictive information beyond metadata.

Under the same cascade structure and tuning protocol, diagnostics improve accuracy from 0.5420.542 to 0.7140.714 and reduce regret from 0.0570.057 to 0.0280.028. Paired 95%95\% intervals for these differences are [0.001,0.346][0.001,0.346] and [−0.054,−0.002][-0.054,-0.002]. The gains persist when any one evaluation group is omitted from the fixed predictions (Appendix A.9).

Diagnostic groups contribute jointly to routing.

Adding any single diagnostic group to metadata yields accuracy of 0.5350.535–0.5490.549, versus 0.7140.714 for Full (Table 16). Removing supervised representation diagnostics or the text diagnostic reduces accuracy to 0.5440.544 or 0.5290.529 and raises regret to 0.1080.108 or 0.1050.105. Removing geometry has a smaller effect, with accuracy 0.6710.671 and regret 0.0410.041. Adding geometry alone slightly increases accuracy over metadata-only (0.5490.549 versus 0.5420.542) but raises regret (0.1130.113 versus 0.0570.057), illustrating that accuracy gains can coexist with more costly errors. All three removals increase mean regret, and the reported paired regret-difference intervals favour Full. These results average five runs with separately sampled text-probe examples.

The cascade improves both stage decisions over Direct.

At ϵ=0\epsilon=0, the cascade reaches 0.8060.806 Step 1 accuracy and 0.8430.843 Step 2 accuracy, with the latter evaluated on settings whose true winner is Joint or Decoupled. Direct reports 0.6540.654 and 0.6270.627 for the corresponding binary decisions on the same evaluation subsets.

Routing accuracy is stable under the tested feature-encoder change.

Replacing the general-domain feature encoders with the base-tier configuration preserves routing accuracy: final accuracy changes from 71.4%71.4\% to 71.8%71.8\%, with Step 1 at 0.8040.804 and Step 2 at 0.8670.867 (Table 17).

Prediction performance varies across implementations.

Direct uses the same feature information, preprocessing, grouped validation, and feature-selection framework as the cascade, but uses a single-stage three-class objective and argmax decisions (Appendix C.9). At ϵ=0\epsilon=0, accuracy/regret is 0.450/0.0910.450/0.091 for Direct and 0.486/0.1270.486/0.127 for TB-Majority. Among six further classifiers, logistic regression (C=0.1C=0.1) performs best at 0.571/0.0860.571/0.086 (Table 15, Appendix A.9). Paired intervals for the cascade comparisons with Direct and TB-Majority appear in Tables 18 and 19.

Higher selection accuracy does not always mean lower regret.

CUB has 27.5%27.5\% selection accuracy but regret of only 0.02840.0284. MELD reaches 64.0%64.0\% accuracy yet incurs 0.11890.1189 regret, above metadata-only's 0.04140.0414 (Table 20). CUB errors overselect Agent at larger budgets, whereas costly MELD errors select Decoupled in k-shot settings. In the inspected CUB, KIBA, and MELD folds, feature selection omits explicit budget descriptors from both cascade stages. Their diagnostics still vary with the labelled subset, but this indirect budget signal coexists with errors in tracking budget-dependent preferences. This observation motivates testing mandatory budget features in future routing variants (Appendix A.11).

4 Related Work

Joint Pretraining, Supervised Fusion, and Post-hoc Alignment. CLIP-style joint pretraining (Radford et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2023; Cherti et al., 2023) and related biomedical, audio, and molecular models (Zhang et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b), together with paired protein–ligand adaptation (Gorantla et al., 2025) motivate Joint. Supervised fusion of frozen representations (Baltrušaitis et al., 2019) motivates Decoupled, while MultiBench and MULTIBENCH++ provide cross-domain fusion benchmarks (Liang et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2026). We compare preferences across three alignment paradigms and test their predictability before target-task adaptation. Our fusion heads include a query-based bridge inspired by frozen-encoder methods (Li et al., 2023).

Post-hoc alignment explicitly builds cross-modal compatibility through lightweight functions (Rosenfeld et al., 2022), projectors, fusion modules, or token-level adaptation (Maniparambil et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Gröger et al., 2025; Kulasekara et al., 2025; Tupakula, 2025; Mahmud et al., 2024), or classification-head prototypes (Méndez et al., 2026).

LLM Composition and Multimodal LLMs. Tool-using LMs compose model outputs at inference (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023). Multimodal LLMs learn modality–language connections through pretraining or instruction tuning (Liu et al., 2023a; Bai et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2023; Gemini Team, Google, 2023; Han et al., 2024), and MMMU evaluates deployed multimodal systems (Yue et al., 2024). Our Agent composes unimodal readouts and available text through a frozen text LLM at inference time.

Selection Before Target-Task Adaptation. Algorithm selection uses instance features (Rice, 1976). Transferability scores rank checkpoints from target representations and labels (Nguyen et al., 2020; You et al., 2021). Multimodal information analysis studies redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy (Liang et al., 2023). At a new target task, we predict the paradigm preference before fitting its candidate heads, using a router trained on outcomes from other datasets.

Representation Geometry and the Modality Gap. Diagnostics include manifold structure (Tenenbaum et al., 2000; Roweis & Saul, 2000), uniformity (Wang & Isola, 2020), anisotropy (Ethayarajh, 2019), neural collapse (Papyan et al., 2020), and intrinsic dimension (Pope et al., 2021). Modality-gap studies examine shared-space separation, training interventions, information imbalance, and semantic compression (Liang et al., 2022; Eslami & de Melo, 2025; Schrodi et al., 2025; Grassucci et al., 2025b; Grassucci et al., 2025a). Spectral similarity characterizes eigenvalue structure, while basis alignment concerns cross-modal correspondence (Sarkar, 2026). Our router uses paired relational features across embedding widths, per-side spectral diagnostics, and task diagnostics for paradigm selection.

5 Conclusion

Multimodal alignment selection involves two distinct questions: which paradigm performs best, and how much its integration contributes beyond the individual components. Our results show why both matter: a winning paradigm can derive much of its performance from one component, while changes in supervision can alter the preferred paradigm. The held-out routing results make representation and task diagnostics useful for narrowing this choice before candidate fitting. Selection errors also differ in utility cost, so winner accuracy and relative regret together characterize the value of that recommendation. This distinction motivates a utility-aware routing objective that weights mistakes by their observed performance gaps. Such an objective would prioritize avoiding costly errors while giving less weight to choices among nearly tied paradigms, a direction for evaluation on held-out datasets. Extending the candidate set to unimodal and LLM-only systems would connect component evaluation directly to routing. Further work can examine incomplete modality correspondences and multimodal instruction tuning (Liu et al., 2023a; Han et al., 2024), and use controlled pretraining comparisons to isolate the contribution of alignment.

AI usage statement

Large language models, including Claude and Codex, were used to assist with writing, literature lookup, and consistency checks across the manuscript, tables, and figures. The LLMs evaluated as Agent controllers are objects of study, distinct from these writing assistants. The authors take responsibility for the experimental evidence, references, and interpretations in the final manuscript.

Reproducibility statement

All datasets and pretrained checkpoints are public (Appendix B). Upon publication, we will release code and records to regenerate the results (Appendix H). Appendices C, E, and D give training details, the Agent prompt, and feature definitions.

Ethics statement

This work benchmarks existing public datasets and pretrained models, and collects no new data from human subjects. Some datasets contain social-media content that may be offensive (CrisisMMD, Memotion, MetMeme), and two contain medical images (Fracture, VQA-RAD). We use every dataset only for the benchmark task its release defines, under its stated licence and access conditions.

Appendix A Additional Results and Ablations

This appendix expands Section 3. Budget curves and seed stability appear in Sections A.1 and A.2. Fusion-head, scaling, and domain-pretraining ablations are in Sections A.3, A.4, and A.5. Sections A.6, A.7, and A.8 examine individual modalities and Agent components. Routing comparisons, utility differences, and task-level failures are in Sections A.9, A.10, and A.11. Section A.12 reports output-format failures.

A.1 Win Map and Label-Budget Curves

Figure 5 shows winners at the three representative budgets in the main tables. Figure 6 traces utility over the full budget grids of six datasets.

A.2 Per-Seed Variance and Winner Stability of the Main Tables

Every Joint and Decoupled entry in Tables 1 and 2 is a mean over 55 seed-specific development-selected models, the seed setting the labelled set below 100%100\% and the head initialisation at every budget. The seed-resolved results used below contain five observations for each configuration, including Agent. Table 4 lists the per-seed standard deviations for the CLS/REG cells, the mean utility gap, and its descriptive status. The better of Joint and Decoupled is decided by the sign of the mean gap, with ties going to Decoupled. A cell is flagged a near-tie if |gap|≤0.005|\mathrm{gap}|\leq 0.005, noisy if the mean winner holds but |gap||\mathrm{gap}| is below the combined standard deviation sJ2+sD2\sqrt{s_{J}^{2}+s_{D}^{2}}, and clear otherwise, as descriptive seed-spread categories rather than significance tests: 2323 cells are clear, 77 noisy, and 33 near-ties. The near-ties are Memotion at 10%10\% and 100%100\% and PDBbind at 100%100\%.

Table 5 reports empirical winner counts from the five corresponding seed scores of all three configurations. Accuracy is maximized and MAE is minimized within each seed. A sole winner receives one win. Configurations tied for best share one win equally, so every row sums to five. The reported scores have three decimal places: equal values are ties at the reported precision, not evidence of statistical equivalence. Across 240240 comparisons, fractional counts are 81.581.5, 87.087.0, and 71.571.5 for Joint, Decoupled, and Agent, respectively. Dividing by five gives seed-averaged counts of 16.316.3, 17.417.4, and 14.314.3 cells, whose sum is 4848. These differ from the 16/18/1416/18/14 mean-utility winner counts because the order of averaging and winner selection differs and this table shares tie credit rather than applying the preference rule. The same configuration is the sole winner in all five seeds in 3838 cells. The other ten show a change of winner or a best-score tie. There are seven tied-best seed comparisons. For example, CrisisMMD at 2020-shot gives 2/0/32/0/3 wins for Joint/Decoupled/Agent, while Memotion at 2020-shot gives 2.5/2.5/02.5/2.5/0. They describe variability across the five runs on fixed test examples. No test examples are resampled in this analysis, so these counts do not quantify test-sampling uncertainty or a probability of winning on future examples.

A.3 Fusion Strategy Ablation

Tables 6 and 7 compare fixed fusion heads at 100%100\% supervision on the default encoder pairs. The main tables instead average seed-specific development-selected heads, so their means can differ from every fixed-head entry. Restricting Joint to a single concat head instead would change the winner on one of the sixteen datasets at 100%100\%, PDBbind (1.160→1.1871.160\to 1.187 MAE), from Joint to Decoupled.

No single head dominates. For Decoupled (Table 6), attention is best on CrisisMMD, Fracture, AI2D and IEMOCAP, mlp on Food101, DrugBank-Desc and KIBA, film on MELD and VQA-RAD, concat on Memotion and PDBbind, bilinear on DrugBank-Pharma and, tied with film, on ScienceQA, gated on MetMeme and add on OxfordPet, and concat and logit_sum tie on CUB, while logit_sum, which only adds readout logits, is weakest on the molecular QA tasks (0.2520.252 on DrugBank-Desc). The preferred heads also differ between paradigms: on ScienceQA, Decoupled reaches 0.7500.750 with either bilinear or film, whereas Joint reaches 0.8220.822 with mlp (Table 7). Across the three reported budgets the best head changes on 1515 of the 1616 dataset–paradigm pairs of the classification datasets, but the spread between the best and the worst head tells where that choice matters: at 100%100\% it is 0.0060.006 to 0.130.13 on classification and 0.110.11 to 0.580.58 on the MCQ tasks, and at 2020-shot it reaches 0.220.22 on Memotion. Figures 7 and 8 show the head choice across budgets and the mean ranks.

A.4 Backbone Scaling Ablation

Figure 9 compares base (∼\sim150M parameters), large (∼\sim430M), and huge (∼\sim990M) towers within the CLIP/SigLIP/EVA02 family. Each tier reports the pair with the highest five-seed test mean, forming a test-oracle envelope rather than the development-selected comparison used in the main benchmark. On CUB, Decoupled wins at the base and large tiers at 100%100\% supervision (Table 8). On Food101, Joint wins at every tier and its lead grows from 0.0460.046 at the base tier to 0.0640.064 at the large tier, because Joint improves (0.8700.870, 0.8830.883) while Decoupled stays flat (0.8240.824, 0.8190.819). The huge tier is a different comparison. No DINOv2 checkpoint exists at that size, so the only unaligned tower matched to OpenCLIP-ViT-H/14 is MAE-ViT-H/14, and Decoupled falls to 0.6590.659 on CUB and 0.6240.624 on Food101. The huge-tier gap therefore reflects a joint change in scale and encoder family.

A.5 Domain Pretraining Ablation

Figure 10 compares general and domain-specific encoders on medical and audio data (setup in Appendix B.5). For Joint on Fracture at 100%100\%, the general CLIP-ViT-B/16 reaches 0.3220.322 and all three biomedical FMs are higher (PLIP 0.3670.367, BiomedCLIP 0.3880.388, PubMedCLIP 0.4190.419), a gain of up to 9.79.7 points. For Decoupled the picture is the opposite: the general DINOv2-B/14 tower (0.4050.405) stays ahead of the radiology and pathology encoders (Rad-DINO 0.3160.316, Phikon 0.3430.343) at almost every budget. On MELD, the general-audio CLAP (0.5710.571) is well ahead of a music-domain CLAP (0.4810.481), a wrong-domain control whose head collapses to the majority class at every percentage budget, and Decoupled leads Joint at every percentage budget with any of the three audio encoders. Changing the encoder configuration affects both absolute accuracy and the system ranking: on Fracture at 100%100\% the default BiomedCLIP trails Decoupled by 0.0170.017 and PubMedCLIP would lead it by 0.0140.014. PubMedCLIP also changes the visual patch size and text architecture relative to the default Decoupled pair (Appendix B.5), so this reversal reflects the full configuration change. At the two smaller Fracture budgets Joint wins with either backbone.

A.6 Single-Modality Probes and the Decoupled Pair

Table 9 places the default Decoupled pair (DINOv2-L/14 + GPT-2) and the base-tier pair (DINOv2-B/14 + BERT-base) beside linear probes of the single frozen encoders and beside the matched Joint FM (CLIP-ViT-L/14). Swapping the default pair for the base-tier pair changes Decoupled by at most 0.0160.016 on CUB, OxfordPet and Food101 at 100%100\%, and by 0.0900.090 on CrisisMMD (0.6280.628 vs. 0.5380.538). The swap changes both towers, and on CrisisMMD the BERT probe (0.5880.588) is also stronger than the GPT-2 probe (0.4710.471).

Modality value and probe budget.

On CUB, the DINOv2-L probe and default Decoupled both reach 0.8990.899 at 2020-shot. At 10%10\% they reach 0.8530.853 and 0.8300.830, and at full budget 0.9160.916 and 0.9170.917. Adding text leaves accuracy unchanged at 2020-shot, lowers it at 10%10\%, and improves it by only 0.10.1 percentage points at full budget. Here 10%10\% supplies only 795795 training labels, whereas 2020-shot supplies 4,0004{,}000 (2020 per class) and full budget 8,2448{,}244 (Table 27), so both scores are lower at 10%10\% than at 2020-shot.

Why a single caption can be difficult to classify.

CUB captions describe visible appearance, such as plumage colour, bill shape, and markings on individual body parts. The caption collection protocol asks annotators not to name the species and does not reveal the species label to them (Reed et al., 2016). Our setup uses only the first of ten captions for each image. A single description can omit distinguishing details, while the attributes it mentions may be shared by several of the 200200 fine-grained bird categories. Identifying the species from that text alone can therefore be difficult, even when the description accurately matches the image. This ambiguity is a plausible contributor to the weak text-only results and the limited gain over the strong visual probe at larger budgets. Text representation and probe training may also contribute to this pattern.

Text-only comparison on Memotion.

On Memotion at 2020-shot, the BERT probe reaches 0.4260.426, above default Decoupled at 0.3490.349. BERT is an alternative text encoder, whereas the default pair uses GPT-2. This comparison shows a competitive single-modality configuration. The comparison varies both modality access and the text encoder.

A.7 Agent Ablations

Three ablations vary one component of the Agent at a time, with Qwen3-32B, Inline-1 and NICL=10N_{\mathrm{ICL}}{=}10 as defaults.

In-context examples (Figure 11).

Table 10 compares NICL=10N_{\mathrm{ICL}}{=}10 in-context examples with none on the eight classification datasets. The mean gain is below one point. The largest gains are on MetMeme at 2020-shot (+0.099+0.099) and CrisisMMD at 100%100\% (+0.049+0.049), and the examples hurt on OxfordPet (−0.057-0.057 at 10%10\%). On MetMeme at 2020-shot, removing demonstrations lowers Agent from 0.2900.290 to 0.1910.191, below Joint at 0.2520.252. On OxfordPet at 10%10\%, removal raises Agent from 0.8410.841 to 0.8980.898, while Decoupled remains ahead at 0.9280.928. The two examples distinguish a reversal of paradigm preference from an accuracy change that preserves the winner.

LLM backbone choice (Figure 12).

Tables 11 and 12 compare Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, Gemma-3-27B-it (Gemma Team, Google DeepMind, 2025), and GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI, 2025) under Inline-1. No backbone dominates: Gemma-3-27B-it is best on CUB and OxfordPet at every budget and Qwen3-32B on Food101. Measured against the better fusion paradigm of Tables 1 and 2, the Agent-versus-fusion preference usually agrees across all four backbones on their shared tasks and budgets. All four win AI2D at 10%10\% and 100%100\%, Food101 at every budget, MELD at 2020-shot, and VQA-RAD at 10%10\%, and none wins any regression, DrugBank, Fracture, Memotion, or OxfordPet cell. Some preferences change with the backbone. Accuracy differences are usually a few points but reach 0.220.22 on CrisisMMD and 0.150.15 on OxfordPet.

Tool-dispatch mode (Figure 13).

Inline-1 pre-computes both readouts and provides them in a single LLM turn. Multi-2 shows the LLM the two tool schemas, lets it call one tool, and takes its answer in a second turn. The additional turn changes the interaction protocol, with computation and latency also depending on token counts and serving conditions. We compare the two on the seven classification datasets for which both readouts were available to the Multi-2 controller. Multi-2 is usually less accurate across the three reported budgets, with a mean gap of −0.136-0.136 (−0.043-0.043 excluding CUB). The controller makes close to one tool call per sample and often picks the uninformative readout: on CUB it calls the text readout on 79%79\% of samples, and accuracy falls from 0.860.86 to 0.160.16 averaged over budgets. OxfordPet loses 0.130.13, Food101, MetMeme, and CrisisMMD lose 0.040.04 to 0.050.05, and Fracture and Memotion change by less than 0.010.01. Inline-1 is the configuration used throughout the main benchmark.

A.8 Agent Prior-Knowledge Controls

To test whether Agent’s accuracy reflects the multimodal readouts or the frozen LLM’s parametric prior, we report five controls under the deployed Qwen3-32B Inline-1 setting at the 100%100\% training budget. LLM-only removes both readouts. Shuffled-tool preserves the readout format but supplies another sample’s readouts (a seeded permutation of the sample-to-readout map). Anonymised labels replaces every class name or MCQ option the LLM sees, in prompts and readouts, by a semantically empty token (class_i, option_j). No demonstrations (classification) / No question (QA) denotes task-specific interventions. For classification, No demonstrations removes the in-context example texts and labels while retaining the current sample text, class names and descriptions, and both readout outputs. On QA tasks, the control deletes only the question body, retaining answer options, instructions, demonstrations, and all other prompt content. All six conditions use the complete test split and the same five-seed aggregation as the corresponding full-budget entries in Tables 1 and 2. Anonymisation retains the question and other sample text.

Relative to LLM-only, the full system changes mean accuracy by −0.052-0.052 on AI2D, +0.014+0.014 on ScienceQA, and +0.075+0.075 on VQA-RAD. It exceeds shuffled-readout performance by 0.1180.118, 0.0790.079, and 0.0750.075, respectively. Thus, sensitivity to readout content can coexist with either positive or negative gains from supplying it. These are five-seed mean contrasts on matched test examples, with uncertainty reporting described in Appendix I.

On CUB and OxfordPet, anonymised labels retain 0.6000.600 and 0.6320.632, compared with 0.0330.033 and 0.2030.203 for LLM-only and 0.0250.025 and 0.2240.224 for shuffled readouts. This indicates useful readout evidence even when label names are unavailable. For MCQ, anonymising options removes their semantic content but retains the question. The No demonstrations / No question column keeps the LLM and readouts. Classification removes only the in-context examples, retaining current sample text and class semantics. QA removes only the question body, retaining all other prompt content. The classification entries reproduce the 100%100\%-budget NICL=0N_{\mathrm{ICL}}{=}0 results in Table 10. Accuracy is 0.6340.634, 0.8720.872, 0.1590.159, 0.2130.213, and 0.9540.954 on CrisisMMD, CUB, Fracture, Memotion, and OxfordPet, and 0.6020.602, 0.5450.545, and 0.2050.205 on AI2D, ScienceQA, and VQA-RAD. The full system exceeds this control by 17.617.6, 13.413.4, and 17.017.0 percentage points on the three QA datasets. Removing demonstrations lowers accuracy on CrisisMMD, CUB, and Memotion, but raises it on Fracture (0.1360.136 to 0.1590.159) and OxfordPet (0.9450.945 to 0.9540.954). Appendix I specifies the inputs retained by each intervention.

For classification, LLM+readouts removes the current sample text, class names and descriptions, and in-context example texts and labels. Readout scores and nonsemantic candidate identifiers remain available to the LLM. The contrast measures the joint removal of direct sample text and label semantics. For QA, the LLM-plus-readouts control retains the controller and readout outputs while removing direct raw sample text, including the question and answer-option contents. Candidate identifiers support answer selection. On the same test examples, this column reports 0.3250.325, 0.4580.458, 0.0820.082, 0.2020.202, 0.1950.195, 0.3250.325, 0.3720.372, and 0.1850.185 in table order. On AI2D, ScienceQA, and VQA-RAD, these accuracies are respectively 27.727.7, 17.317.3, and 2.02.0 percentage points below the question-body-ablation column. The two columns distinguish question removal from removal of all direct text content.

Score averaging.

Table 14 compares two interventions: its upper panel removes the LLM on the Agent-winning settings of CrisisMMD, Food101, MELD, and MetMeme, while its lower panel removes the readouts on Food101 at three budgets. Averaging the class probabilities of the two readouts reaches roughly the stronger readout, which is near or below Decoupled, and stays 9.69.6 to 24.924.9 points below Agent in each reported setting. The text readout is below Agent on all four datasets, whereas the LLM reads the raw text of the sample. The full system combines raw-text access and LLM-mediated use of readouts, and outperforms probability averaging in these comparisons. For Food101, averaging reaches 0.6950.695, 0.7370.737, and 0.8100.810 at 2020-shot, 10%10\%, and full budget, versus 0.8720.872, 0.8800.880, and 0.9060.906 for Agent. The listed single-modality probes in Table 9 also remain below Agent. LLM-only reaches 0.8430.843, 0.8520.852, and 0.8980.898, giving full-system-minus-LLM-only gains of 0.0290.029, 0.0280.028, and 0.0080.008. These conditional input contrasts retain the LLM and raw-text access, and extend the readout intervention to both smaller and full training budgets. LLM-only, the listed probes and readouts, and probability averaging do not overturn the three reported Agent wins on Food101. The small full-budget mean gain qualifies its practical magnitude. Uncertainty reporting follows Appendix I.

Same-size controller.

With SmolLM2-135M-Instruct as controller, at or below the scale of the encoder towers, and the Inline-1 protocol unchanged, Agent never outperforms the better fusion paradigm in the evaluated classification and QA settings, whereas Qwen3-8B does so in some of these settings. Its mean parse-failure rate over these evaluations is near 0.90.9, so the 135135M model does not follow the answer protocol.

A.9 Grouped Routing Comparison

The reference TB-Majority assigns the majority winner among outer-training cells sharing task type and budget type. Direct classification and the cascade instead use the diagnostic and metadata features in Appendix D.1. All three are evaluated on the same 144144 cells in 1515 groups, with DrugBank-Desc and DrugBank-Pharma held out together. Results average five labelled-set feature runs.

Additional routing classifiers.

Table 15 compares six additional configurations: logistic regression with stronger regularization (C=0.1C=0.1), shrinkage LDA, 55-NN, an RBF-kernel SVM, naive Bayes with missing-value support, and depth-22 histogram gradient boosting. Logistic regression achieves the highest accuracy (0.5710.571) and lowest relative regret (0.0860.086) among these alternatives. The table’s intervals concern accuracy differences from TB-Majority and are available for logistic regression and gradient boosting, both spanning zero. Cascade–classifier intervals were not computed.

Metadata-only reference.

The metadata-only baseline retains the cascade protocol and removes only diagnostic features (Appendix C.10). At ϵ=0\epsilon=0, it reports 0.5420.542 accuracy, 78.078.0 correctly selected cells averaged over five runs, and 0.05660.0566 mean relative regret. Relative to this baseline, the full cascade selects 24.824.8 more cells correctly on average and lowers mean regret by 0.02830.0283, approximately 50%50\%. Table 20 provides the per-dataset comparison. At the displayed precision, the cascade has lower regret on eight datasets, equal regret on four, and higher regret on four (CUB, KIBA, MELD, and PDBbind). Grouping the two DrugBank tasks together gives eight improvements, three ties, and four regressions over the 1515 evaluation groups. These are descriptive comparisons of mean regret at zero tolerance. Table 3 reports all five tolerances.

Diagnostic feature-group ablations.

Table 16 complements Full versus metadata-only with single-group additions and removals. The text diagnostic is Δzs\Delta_{\mathrm{zs}}. None of the single-group additions recovers Full’s accuracy or regret. The largest accuracy reductions occur when supervised representation diagnostics or the text diagnostic is removed. Geometry removal produces a smaller mean accuracy reduction, whose interval includes zero, but increases regret. The accuracy interval for text-diagnostic removal also includes zero, whereas the regret intervals for all three removals favour Full. These paired comparisons describe the contribution of each group in the presence of the remaining features.

Sensitivity to individual evaluation groups.

For the Full-minus-metadata-only comparison at ϵ=0\epsilon=0, paired dataset-group bootstrap resampling draws 1515 groups with replacement, keeping both DrugBank tasks in one group and all budget cells and five seed rows together. Each draw uses the same groups for both methods and computes the cell-weighted difference. We use 4,0004{,}000 draws with NumPy default_rng(0) and report the 2.52.5th and 97.597.5th percentiles. Accuracy is 0.7138890.713889 versus 0.5416670.541667, giving +0.172222+0.172222 with interval [0.001449,0.345991][0.001449,0.345991]. Relative regret is 0.0283380.028338 versus 0.0566010.056601, giving −0.028263-0.028263 with interval [−0.054377,−0.002035][-0.054377,-0.002035]. These group-level intervals condition on the fitted held-out predictions and candidate utilities.

At ϵ=0\epsilon=0, we hold the existing five-run outer-held-out predictions fixed and omit each of the 1515 evaluation groups in turn from the aggregate, treating the two DrugBank tasks as one group. We recompute cell-weighted Cascade-minus-metadata-only differences on the remaining 1414 groups. For group gg with ngn_{g} cells and mean difference δg\delta_{g}, the omitted-group difference is ∑h≠gnh​δh/∑h≠gnh\sum_{h\neq g}n_{h}\delta_{h}/\sum_{h\neq g}n_{h}. Accuracy differences use correct-count increments implied by five runs and the displayed cell counts, consistent with the reported totals 102.8102.8 and 78.078.0.

The full-set accuracy difference is 24.8/144=0.172224.8/144=0.1722. After omitting any one group, accuracy differences range from +0.117+0.117 to +0.204+0.204, and relative-regret differences range from −0.036-0.036 to −0.020-0.020. Omitting VQA-RAD gives the smallest accuracy advantage, (24.8−9)/(144−9)=0.1170(24.8-9)/(144-9)=0.1170, while omitting KIBA gives the largest, (24.8+2.6)/(144−10)=0.2045(24.8+2.6)/(144-10)=0.2045. The most negative regret difference occurs without MELD, and the least negative without VQA-RAD. Across individual groups, accuracy improves/ties/worsens in 10/3/210/3/2 groups. Regret improves/ties/worsens in 8/3/48/3/4. Thus the direction of the aggregate advantage does not depend on any single evaluation group, although gains vary across tasks.

A.10 Utility-Based Routing Comparison

Tables 18 and 19 complement the mean results in Table 3 with paired differences and pointwise bootstrap intervals. At the reference tolerance, all four intervals exclude zero in favour of the cascade. The lower bound against TB-Majority is close to zero. At the other four tolerances, accuracy intervals against TB-Majority cross zero, indicating uncertainty in the direction of the accuracy difference at those tolerances. The comparison evaluates each complete predictor, including its feature access and decision rule.

Across the five tie bands, mean accuracy/regret is 0.678/0.0450.678/0.045 for the cascade, 0.498/0.0880.498/0.088 for direct classification, and 0.503/0.1270.503/0.127 for TB-Majority, computed from the displayed summaries. Direct classification has lower accuracy than TB-Majority at the first three bands and higher accuracy at the last two, while its regret is lower throughout. The cascade has lower mean regret than direct classification at every reported tolerance. Larger tolerances do not necessarily improve prediction or utility.

A.11 Per-Dataset Routing Results

Table 20 reports all 1616 tasks at the reference tolerance. The cascade attains perfect winner accuracy on AI2D, both DrugBank tasks, and VQA-RAD, but its accuracy is only 0.2750.275 on CUB, 0.2800.280 on ScienceQA, and 0.3200.320 on Memotion. Every dataset has nonzero accuracy after averaging the five runs. Relative regret is largest on MELD (0.11890.1189), Memotion (0.11110.1111), and ScienceQA (0.11070.1107). TB-Majority is better on both metrics for CUB, MELD, and KIBA, has lower regret but lower accuracy on IEMOCAP, and higher accuracy but higher regret on Memotion. The aggregate advantage thus coexists with task-specific reversals. On ScienceQA, the displayed regret is identical for all three methods despite different winner accuracy, further illustrating that these metrics capture different aspects of selection.

Stage-specific failure patterns.

The fold-level diagnostic inspection identifies different failure modes on CUB, KIBA, and MELD. On CUB, errors arise at the Agent/Fusion decision: the router continues to favor Agent at larger budgets where Decoupled is preferred. The text diagnostic Δzs\Delta_{\mathrm{zs}} remains positive across budgets (approximately 0.040.04–0.190.19), but this proxy is not a measured Agent–fusion utility difference. The five-run aggregate relative regret is 0.02840.0284, illustrating that frequent winner errors can have a modest average utility cost. On KIBA, the Agent/Fusion decision correctly rejects Agent. The reported errors instead concern Joint/Decoupled choices in the k-shot regime. Small fusion-utility differences in most of these cells limit the aggregate regret to 0.01030.0103.

On MELD, the diagnostic inspection identifies costly k-shot errors in which the router selects Decoupled despite a substantial Agent advantage. Its text diagnostic is near zero in the reported cells (approximately −0.04-0.04 to 0.130.13). A possible explanation is a mismatch between text–label matching in the fixed BGE probe and the controller’s ability to interpret transcripts. Under the reported five-run aggregation, the full router has slightly higher accuracy than metadata-only (0.6400.640 versus 0.6000.600), but higher regret (0.11890.1189 versus 0.04140.0414). Its mistakes therefore incur greater utility loss on average.

In the inspected CUB, KIBA, and MELD folds, inner selection excludes the explicit budget block from both stages of the full router, while the metadata-only reference retains budget descriptors. The full router consequently lacks a direct budget covariate in these folds, although its diagnostic features can still vary with the labelled subset and thus indirectly convey budget information. This selection pattern is consistent with difficulty tracking budget-dependent winner changes. Together, these cases distinguish errors at the Agent/Fusion boundary from errors between fusion systems, and show why similar winner accuracy can conceal very different utility losses.

A.12 Regression Output Parsing

Table 21 reports default-AGENT parsing failures. Rates are 0.10.1–0.2%0.2\% on IEMOCAP, 0.30.3–2.9%2.9\% on KIBA, and 2.82.8–3.3%3.3\% on PDBbind. Under the zero-substitution rule, the reported MAE includes both prediction error and output-format failures. The MAE contribution of each parsing failure depends on the distance between zero and the target value. These are end-to-end system results. Conditional MAE on parsed outputs cannot be reconstructed from failure percentages alone.

A.13 Sensitivity of the Descriptive Joint–Decoupled Association

Figure 4A counts Joint–Decoupled preferences across every budget of each QA dataset, regardless of Agent's rank. Here nn denotes the number of budgets, not independent datasets.

Here uu is the raw knn5_mod_max diagnostic: the larger of the two modalities’ five-seed mean leave-one-out kNN-5 accuracies (Eq. (17)), before any size residualization. We first average within each modality, then take the maximum. The margin uses direction-adjusted utilities from Eq. (1):

u⁡(d,K)\displaystyle u(d,K) =maxm∈{a,b}⁡{15​∑s=04akNN5,m(s)​(d,K)},\displaystyle=\max_{m\in\{a,b\}}\left\{\frac{1}{5}\sum_{s=0}^{4}a_{\mathrm{kNN5},m}^{(s)}(d,K)\right\},
mJ​(d,K)\displaystyle m_{J}(d,K) =U⁡(Joint,d,K)−U⁡(Decoupled,d,K)|U⋆​(d,K)|.\displaystyle=\frac{U(\textsc{Joint};d,K)-U(\textsc{Decoupled};d,K)}{|U^{\star}(d,K)|}.

where U⋆=max⁡{U⁡(Agent),U⁡(Joint),U⁡(Decoupled)}U^{\star}=\max\{U(\textsc{Agent}),U(\textsc{Joint}),U(\textsc{Decoupled})\}. Thus the denominator includes Agent: it scales the Joint–Decoupled difference by the best of all three configurations. It does not change which fusion configuration wins, but can affect cross-dataset margin magnitudes and ranks. The plotted margin averages cell-wise ratios over budgets.

For Figure 4B, each of the eight classification datasets contributes one point, with equal weight. We average uu and the Joint–Decoupled margin over identical cells with available uu: 8484 of 8585 classification cells. Memotion’s one-shot cell lacks uu and is excluded from both means. The matched-cell Spearman correlation is −0.667-0.667. The leave-one-dataset-out sensitivity range is [−0.750,−0.571][-0.750,-0.571], obtained by recomputing the descriptive correlation on each remaining set of seven datasets. If the margin mean instead includes every budget cell, the correlation becomes −0.738-0.738. Only Memotion changes, reversing its margin rank relative to Food101. Using chance-normalized separability (u−1/C)/(1−1/C)(u-1/C)/(1-1/C) with matched cells gives −0.619-0.619, for class counts CC of 77, 1010, 55, 88, 77, 101101, 200200, and 3737 on MetMeme, Fracture, Memotion, CrisisMMD, MELD, Food101, CUB, and OxfordPet, respectively. Across these checks, the association remains negative, while its magnitude varies with the ranks of the eight datasets.
